questions.prompt: What is compound interest?
choices: Interest paid only on the original amount
Interest earned on both the principal and prior interest
A fee the bank charges for holding your money
The interest rate on a loan
questions.explanation: Compound interest grows your money faster because prior interest also earns interest.

questions.prompt: If you invest $100 at 10% interest compounded annually, roughly how much do you have after 2 years?
Why do investors say 'time in the market beats timing the market'?
choices: Because markets only go up
Because consistent long-term investing usually outperforms trying to guess the best moments to buy and sell
Because brokers charge less on long holds
Because there is no tax on long-term gains
questions.explanation: Trying to predict short-term moves is hard; long-term growth plus compounding is usually more reliable.

questions.prompt: Diversification means:
choices: Putting all your money in one hot stock
Spreading your money across different investments to lower risk
Only buying bonds
Buying and selling as fast as possible
questions.explanation: If one investment drops, others may hold steady, reducing your overall risk.

questions.prompt: What is a stock?
choices: A loan you give to a company
A share of ownership in a company
A government savings bond
A type of insurance policy
questions.explanation: Buying a stock makes you a partial owner of that company.

questions.prompt: Opportunity cost is:
choices: The fee a broker charges per trade
The value of the next best choice you gave up
The cost of insurance
The interest on a credit card
questions.explanation: Spending $500 on an upgrade means giving up whatever that $500 could have earned if invested.

questions.prompt: Which typically has higher long-term return but also higher short-term risk?
choices: A savings account
A certificate of deposit
A diversified stock index fund
A checking account
questions.explanation: Stocks bounce around more day to day, but on average they grow faster over decades.

questions.prompt: A dividend is:
choices: A portion of a company's earnings paid to shareholders
A loan from a company
A tax on profit
A discount on future stock purchases
questions.explanation: Some companies share profits with their shareholders via dividends.

questions.prompt: A bear market is:
choices: A period when prices are generally rising
A period when prices are generally falling
A market that only sells agricultural goods
A market with only small companies
questions.explanation: Bears swipe down, bulls thrust up -- easy way to remember.

questions.prompt: If you buy a stock at $10 and sell it at $12, your return is:
questions.explanation: You gained $2 on a $10 investment: 2/10 = 20%.

questions.prompt: Which statement about risk is TRUE?
choices: Higher risk always means higher reward
Riskier investments have a wider range of outcomes, both up and down
Cash has zero risk
Risk only matters for day traders
questions.explanation: Risk is about uncertainty -- you might do much better, but you might also lose more.

questions.prompt: The 'time value of money' says:
choices: A dollar today is worth more than a dollar in the future
A dollar in the future is worth more than a dollar today
Money is always worth the same no matter when you get it
Inflation does not affect money
questions.explanation: A dollar today can be invested and grow; a future dollar cannot.

questions.prompt: Dollar-cost averaging means:
choices: Trading on margin to amplify returns
Investing a fixed amount on a regular schedule regardless of price
Buying only when prices hit a low
Splitting investments equally between stocks and bonds
questions.explanation: You buy more shares when prices are low and fewer when they are high -- smooths out timing risk.

questions.prompt: Which of these is generally the SAFEST place to hold short-term savings?
choices: Individual tech stocks
Crypto
A high-yield savings account
Options contracts
questions.explanation: Savings accounts are insured and stable, suited for money you might need soon.

questions.prompt: Inflation means:
choices: Prices generally rising over time
Prices generally falling over time
A tax on savings
The stock market going up
questions.explanation: At 3% inflation, $100 today buys roughly $97 worth of goods next year.

questions.prompt: Why does compound interest favor starting early?
choices: Because interest rates are lower when you are young
Because you have more years for interest to earn its own interest
Because brokers give discounts to teenagers
Because young investors pay less tax
questions.explanation: An extra decade of compounding often matters more than investing larger amounts later.

questions.prompt: An index fund is:
choices: A hand-picked portfolio managed by a star investor
A fund that tracks a broad market index like the S&P 500
A government-issued bond
A crypto wallet
questions.explanation: Index funds are low-cost and broadly diversified -- a common default for long-term investors.

questions.prompt: Selling an investment to lock in a gain is called:
choices: Shorting
Realizing a gain
Hedging
Rebalancing
questions.explanation: Paper gains become real only when you sell -- that is 'realizing' them.

questions.prompt: A portfolio heavily weighted toward one stock is:
choices: Well diversified
Concentrated -- higher risk
Guaranteed to outperform
Tax-free
questions.explanation: If that single stock drops, most of your portfolio drops with it.

questions.prompt: You have $1,000 and two choices: spend it on a restaurant upgrade that adds $50/day income, or invest it at 10% annual return. What concept best captures this tradeoff?
choices: Diversification
Opportunity cost
Inflation
Liquidity
questions.explanation: The cost of choosing the upgrade is the return you gave up by not investing.

questions.prompt: Insurance is designed to:
choices: Guarantee a profit
Protect you from large financial losses by spreading risk
Replace the need for savings
Pay you each month whether something happens or not
questions.explanation: You pay a small premium to avoid a potentially huge bill later.

questions.prompt: A premium is:
choices: The amount the insurer pays you after a claim
The amount you pay regularly to keep coverage active
The fee a doctor charges for an exam
The tax on insurance
questions.explanation: Miss your premium and coverage can lapse -- exposing you to the full loss.

questions.prompt: A deductible is:
choices: The total value of your policy
The amount you pay out of pocket before insurance starts paying
A discount on your premium
A tax write-off
questions.explanation: Higher deductible = lower premium, but more out-of-pocket if something happens.

questions.prompt: If a loss is less than your deductible, insurance typically:
choices: Pays the full amount anyway
Pays nothing -- you cover it yourself
Pays half
Refunds your premium
questions.explanation: Small losses are your responsibility; insurance kicks in above the deductible.

questions.prompt: A claim is:
choices: A marketing pitch from the insurer
A request for the insurer to pay for a covered loss
The monthly premium
An annual review
questions.explanation: You file a claim when a covered event happens, then the insurer pays per the policy terms.

questions.prompt: Why do insurance companies usually charge higher premiums for riskier customers?
choices: They dislike risky customers
Because expected payouts are higher, and premiums must reflect expected losses
Because regulation requires it
Because risky customers have more money
questions.explanation: Insurance pricing reflects the probability and size of expected claims.

questions.prompt: Going uninsured against a catastrophic event is generally:
choices: A smart way to save money
Acceptable because they never happen
Risky -- a single event can wipe out your savings
Required by law
questions.explanation: Insurance exists specifically for events too big to self-fund.

questions.prompt: Liability insurance covers:
choices: Damage to your own property
Harm or losses you cause to others
Dental visits
Lost wages from sickness
questions.explanation: Liability protects your assets if you are found responsible for someone else's loss.

questions.prompt: Raising your deductible usually:
choices: Raises your premium
Lowers your premium
Has no effect on premium
Cancels the policy
questions.explanation: You are taking on more of the small-loss risk, so the insurer charges less.

questions.prompt: Coverage limits are:
choices: The maximum the insurer will pay on a claim
The amount of the premium
The legal age to buy insurance
A limit on how many policies you can own
questions.explanation: Losses above the limit come out of your own pocket.

questions.prompt: Property insurance on a business protects against:
choices: Employees quitting
Physical damage or loss to the building, equipment, and inventory
Declining stock prices
Bad customer reviews
questions.explanation: Fire, storms, theft -- events that damage things you own.

questions.prompt: Pooling of risk means:
choices: Insurers swim together for lower premiums
Many people pay small premiums so a few who suffer losses can be made whole
All insurers set the same price
Only wealthy people can buy insurance
questions.explanation: Insurance works because losses happen to a small fraction of the group each year.

questions.prompt: If you pay $100/month for insurance and never file a claim, is the premium 'wasted'?
choices: Yes -- you should cancel
No -- you bought protection from a large loss you did not end up needing
Yes -- unless you get it refunded
No -- insurers refund unused premiums annually
questions.explanation: Insurance is peace of mind against worst-case scenarios, not a savings product.

questions.prompt: An exclusion in an insurance policy is:
choices: A type of premium discount
Something the policy specifically does not cover
A required add-on
A claim form
questions.explanation: Always read what is excluded -- floods and earthquakes are often excluded from standard property policies.

questions.prompt: Over-insuring means:
choices: Paying premiums larger than the potential loss justifies
Having multiple policies that all pay at once
Insuring only half your asset's value
Insuring something you do not own
questions.explanation: Insurance should be matched to the real financial risk, not every possible bad outcome.

questions.prompt: If a restaurant you own has a fire and is insured, insurance typically pays:
choices: Nothing, because fires are excluded by default
The repair cost minus your deductible, up to the policy limit
Three times the property value
Only if you file a lawsuit
questions.explanation: Policies pay the actual covered loss, minus the deductible, capped at the limit.

questions.prompt: The main reason a growing business should consider MORE insurance is:
choices: More revenue means higher mandatory premiums
More assets and more exposure to lawsuits mean larger potential losses
Insurers refuse to work with small businesses
Premiums drop as the business grows
questions.explanation: As your business grows, the size of a possible loss grows with it.

questions.prompt: A 'peril' in insurance language is:
choices: A celebrity endorsement
A specific cause of loss, like fire or theft
A type of premium
A waiting period
questions.explanation: Named-peril policies only cover specific causes listed in the policy.

questions.prompt: If your property's value rises but your coverage limit does not, you may be:
choices: Over-insured
Under-insured -- a total loss would not be fully covered
Due a premium refund
Required to cancel the policy
questions.explanation: Review limits periodically so a total loss does not leave a funding gap.

questions.prompt: Which scenario best captures the value of insurance?
choices: Small, certain cost traded for protection against a large, uncertain loss
Large, certain profit for doing nothing
A guaranteed discount on future purchases
Free replacement of anything you break
questions.explanation: Insurance is exchanging many small predictable payments for protection against rare big losses.

questions.prompt: APR stands for:
choices: Actual Payment Rate
Annual Percentage Rate
Accumulated Principal Rate
Adjustable Payment Requirement
questions.explanation: APR is the yearly cost of borrowing, expressed as a percentage of the balance.

questions.prompt: Paying only the minimum on a credit card each month usually:
choices: Pays off the balance quickly
Saves interest
Takes years and costs a lot in interest
Has no effect on what you owe
questions.explanation: Minimums barely cover the interest; the principal shrinks slowly and interest piles up.

questions.prompt: Your credit score is mostly affected by:
choices: How much you earn
Payment history and how much of your credit you use
Your age
How many bank accounts you have
questions.explanation: On-time payments and low utilization are the biggest drivers of a good score.

questions.prompt: Credit utilization is:
choices: The percentage of your available credit you are currently using
The number of credit cards you own
The interest rate on your card
Your monthly payment
questions.explanation: Lower utilization (often under 30%) usually helps your score.

questions.prompt: Principal on a loan means:
choices: The head of the bank
The original amount borrowed, not including interest
The interest rate
The total cost of the loan
questions.explanation: Each payment goes partly to principal (lowers what you owe) and partly to interest (cost of borrowing).

questions.prompt: A loan with a 5-year term vs. a 15-year term at the same APR:
choices: 5-year: lower monthly payment, less total interest
15-year: lower monthly payment, more total interest
15-year: same total interest as 5-year
There is no difference
questions.explanation: Longer terms cost less each month but more overall because interest compounds over more years.

questions.prompt: A missed loan payment typically causes:
choices: Nothing bad if it is only one
Late fees and potential damage to your credit score
An automatic refund
Principal forgiveness
questions.explanation: Payment history is the biggest factor in credit scores -- one miss can hurt for years.

questions.prompt: Secured vs. unsecured credit: secured debt is:
choices: Backed by collateral the lender can take if you default
Impossible to default on
Always interest-free
Only available to corporations
questions.explanation: A car loan is secured by the car; an unpaid credit card is unsecured.

questions.prompt: A good reason to take on debt is:
choices: To buy depreciating luxuries you cannot afford
To fund an investment or asset expected to earn more than the interest cost
To avoid paying cash for coffee
Because borrowing is free
questions.explanation: If your asset earns more than the loan costs, debt can be a lever. If it earns less, debt hurts you.

questions.prompt: Credit card interest is typically:
choices: Lower than auto loans
Much higher than most other consumer loans
Always 0%
The same as a mortgage
questions.explanation: Credit card APRs commonly range from 15% to 30% or more.

questions.prompt: A down payment is:
choices: The first monthly payment on a loan
Money you pay upfront, reducing the amount you need to borrow
A fee paid to your bank
The interest rate on a loan
questions.explanation: Larger down payments shrink the loan and usually get you a better rate.

questions.prompt: Refinancing a loan means:
choices: Taking out a new loan to replace an existing one, often at better terms
Missing a payment on purpose
Declaring bankruptcy
Paying interest only
questions.explanation: If interest rates drop, refinancing can lower your payments or total interest.

questions.prompt: Defaulting on a loan means:
choices: Paying it off early
Failing to make payments as agreed
Refinancing at a lower rate
Asking for a new credit limit
questions.explanation: Defaults can lead to collections, seizure of collateral, and major credit damage.

questions.prompt: Why does a higher credit score help you?
choices: It guarantees you free loans
Lenders offer you lower interest rates and better terms
You do not need insurance anymore
It raises your income
questions.explanation: Better scores signal lower risk, so lenders compete for your business with better rates.

questions.prompt: The total cost of a loan is best understood by looking at:
choices: Only the monthly payment
The APR plus fees across the full term of the loan
The first year of payments only
The minimum payment listed on the statement
questions.explanation: Monthly payment alone hides how much you pay in interest over time.

questions.prompt: Maxing out a credit card (using nearly all of your limit) usually:
choices: Improves your score by showing active use
Hurts your score because utilization is very high
Has no effect
Unlocks a lower interest rate
questions.explanation: High utilization signals stress on your finances to lenders.

questions.prompt: A business loan vs. a credit card for a large purchase:
choices: Credit cards almost always cost less
A structured business loan often has a lower APR and clear payoff plan
Credit cards must always be used for business
They are identical products
questions.explanation: For big, planned expenses, a loan with a fixed term usually beats carrying credit card debt.

questions.prompt: If you have $1,000 extra and a credit card debt at 20% APR, the highest-return move is usually:
choices: Invest in a stock hoping for a 10% return
Pay down the 20% debt -- a guaranteed 'return' equal to the APR
Leave the money in checking
Buy a lottery ticket
questions.explanation: Eliminating a 20% interest cost is like earning a guaranteed 20% -- hard to beat.

questions.prompt: Amortization is:
choices: A formula for paying off a loan over time with equal periodic payments
The penalty for missing a payment
The interest-only period of a loan
A type of insurance
questions.explanation: Early payments are mostly interest; later payments mostly principal.

questions.prompt: You want to buy a rival-owned lot for $1,500. You have $700 in checking. The smartest first step is usually:
choices: Finance the purchase with a loan you can realistically repay
Max out a credit card for the $800 gap
Skip the purchase entirely forever
Sell all your investments in a panic
questions.explanation: A planned loan with manageable payments is usually cheaper and less risky than high-APR credit card debt.
